explanation: Portuguese marmelada was a firm paste of marmelos, quinces. In English the word moved to citrus preserves, above all bitter Seville orange marmalade.

claims.text: The word marmalade comes from the Portuguese marmelada, from marmelo, meaning quince.
The Portuguese source of 'marmalade' is not the word for orange, lemon or fig.
Portuguese marmelada is a firm quince paste.
In English, marmalade came to mean a preserve of citrus fruit, classically made with bitter Seville oranges.
